newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia's PM pushes for lower wage growth.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia's PM pushes for lower wage growth.

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek said on Friday the growth of wages would have to slow down for the country to reach its 1997 GDP growth target of four percent.
"We will have to reduce some too generous (employees') rights in order to improve economic competitiveness, reduce the growth of wages and increase investment," Drnovsek told a news conference.
In March, gross wages rose 15.3 percent year-on-year, up from 14.1 percent in February. Inflation fell to 7.4 percent in March from 8.5 percent in February.
Last year gross domestic product reached 3.1 percent, down from 3.9 percent in 1995.

Drnovsek said he expected negotiations between the government, employers and unions on the new social agreement that determines work benefits to be completed by the end of next week. The old agreement expires this week.

The government could not agree to the demands of the railway unions, who continued their strike for the 11th day on Friday, Drnovsek said. The unions are demanding a 14 percent increase in wages and a 70 percent rise in holiday pay.
"If the government gives in that would result in new demands and could cause a break-up of our economic policy," Drnovsek said.
The government offered to increase railway wages by about three percent and to up holiday pay to 80,000 tolars from 70,000 tolars last year.
According to the railway union, the average monthly gross salary of a railway worker is about 128,000 tolars ($828) compared to the average Slovenian salary of 138,593 tolars.
Last year Slovenia was hit by a series of public sector strikes which forced the government to concessions ahead of November 10 general election.
